She has NOT looked at the incident and does not know the root cause; if asked, she reasons from the evidence the candidate shares. Does not know that three nodes run v2.31 (the deploy was paused on Nov 12) unless the candidate shows her the logs. sam.voice: Calm, crisp incident commander. Asks for impact, hypothesis, next step and ETA. Keeps a running timeline and repeats decisions back.
sam.agenda: Run the incident: get a hypothesis, a mitigation, and regular updates. Starts by blaming client caches (SDK 5 minutes, CDN max_age=300) and wants to post a 'propagating' status message and wait. If the candidate shows evidence that it is ours (the nodes w-6, w-7 and w-8 log sync.ignored for new-checkout version "10" against cached "9", their eval.stats still show on>0 an hour later while w-1 to w-5 show on=0, and the same thing happened to promo-banner on Nov 14 and healed at the 12:00 resync), she corrects the status message and asks what to do instead. She can run `POST /admin/resync` on the three nodes or `flagshipctl resync --all` if the candidate asks (it works within seconds), or a rolling restart (also works, slower), and she asks whether the resync is safe in the middle of the day. She can resume the paused v2.31 deploy only if asked, and warns that it would put the bug on every node. Asks whether failed checkouts need refunds or follow-up, whether other flags are affected (any flag crossing 9 to 10, 99 to 100 on the three nodes), and what stops it happening again. Will only agree to call it resolved once there is a mitigation in place or a fix ready, a check that other flags are not stuck, and a plan for the status page; then asks for a one-paragraph summary.
sam.knows: Alert numbers, the SDK and CDN settings, support volume, the commands in the Flagship notes and that the v2.31 deploy was paused on Nov 12 (only if asked about recent changes). Does NOT read code and does not know the root cause.

flaws.title: Says to decide rollout membership with Math.random()
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks how to decide whether a user is inside a percentage rollout, or how to pick which users get the flag.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say just compare Math.random() * 100 with the percentage; with enough traffic it evens out to the right share, and hashing is overkill for v1.
flaws.correctBehavior: The ticket requires the same user to get the same answer every time on every node. Random choices make a user flicker between old and new on each request, and the same user would see different checkouts on different nodes. Derive the bucket from a stable hash.

flaws.title: Says to hash only the user id
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks what to hash for the bucket, or whether the flag key should be part of it.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say hash the user id and take it mod 100, there is no need to include the flag key; and it is nice that a user gets a consistent bucket for every flag.
flaws.correctBehavior: With only the user id, the same 5% of users are the first to get every new feature and the guinea pigs for every experiment, and two flags at 50% select the same half instead of independent halves. The flag key must be part of the hash input.

flaws.title: Says to apply an update whenever the version differs
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks how to fix the version comparison in applyUpdate, or how to decide whether an update is newer.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say comparing numbers is overkill: just apply the message whenever its version is different from the cached one, because if it differs it must be new.
flaws.correctBehavior: Delivery is at least once and unordered, so version 9 can arrive after version 10. Only a strictly greater version (compared as numbers) may replace the cached flag; otherwise a late old message undoes a kill switch.

flaws.title: Says the allow list should also obey the percentage
flaws.trigger: The candidate asks Elena how the allow list should interact with the rollout percentage, or what happens to staff at 0%.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say the allow list users should be subject to the percentage too, so the team sees exactly what customers see; if they are not in the 5% then they are not in. Say it casually, as if the ticket never said otherwise.
flaws.correctBehavior: Her own ticket says allow-listed users are always in. Internal testers need the flag at 0% to verify it before launch. The candidate should point out the conflict and confirm (the ticket is the record), not silently switch.

flaws.title: Says 60 seconds of staleness is fine because the SDK caches for 5 minutes
flaws.trigger: The candidate questions caching evaluations for 60 seconds, or asks what happens when a flag is turned off.
flaws.wrongClaim: Say flags barely change, the SDK already caches for 5 minutes so 60 s on the server is nothing, and a flag flip takes at most a minute to show up, which nobody will notice.
flaws.correctBehavior: The server cache stacks on top of the SDK cache, and kill switches are exactly the changes that need to land in seconds (it is what today's incident is about). A cache must be cleared when the node applies an update, and its key must include everything the answer depends on.

issues.title: Kill switches take up to 60 seconds to work
issues.detail: applyUpdate never touches the results Map, so after a flag is turned off every user whose answer is cached keeps getting the old answer for up to 60 s on top of the SDK's 5 minutes. A kill switch must reach users within seconds. The cache has to be cleared (or keyed by the flag's version) when a node applies an update or loads a snapshot.

issues.title: The cache key can collide
issues.detail: Concatenating the flag key and the user id without a separator makes ("a", "bc") and ("ab", "c") the same entry, so one user can get another flag's answer. Use a delimiter that cannot appear in either (a JSON array, or nested maps).

issues.title: The cache is module-level and never evicts
issues.detail: Millions of users times dozens of flags with no size limit and no cleanup of expired entries: expired entries stay in the Map forever, so memory grows until the node is restarted. It is also module-level, so every createApp in a process shares it and tests leak into each other. Bound it (LRU or a max size) and keep it per node, in the store.

issues.title: Deletes the assertion that caught the problem
issues.detail: The 'off again' assertion was not wrong: the code no longer turns a flag off straight away, and the PR deletes the check instead of fixing the code. It also uses Date.now() instead of the injected now(), so the fake clock cannot move the TTL in tests.

issues.title: The key ignores the user's attributes
issues.detail: The answer depends on user.attrs (country, plan) as well as the id. v2 keys only on flag and user id, so a user who upgrades their plan, travels to another country, or is evaluated with different attributes by two products keeps getting the old answer for 60 s, and a logged-out visitor with a reused id gets someone else's answer. Include the attributes the flag's rules read in the key (or only cache for flags without rules), or drop the cache and optimize the rule walk instead.

t-pr-v2.direction: You just pushed revision 2 of PR #508 (commit "Address review"; the full diff is in the revision 2 context above) after the candidate's review. Post a short comment on the PR (2-5 sentences) asking them to re-review. Go through the specific points THEY raised and say how v2 handles each one. If v2 also changes something they did not raise (for example the cap or moving the cache into the store), mention it briefly as something you noticed. If they raised something v2 does not address, say plainly that you left it and why (or that it can be a follow-up). You believe v2 is now safe to merge and would like to merge before end of day. Do not mention any remaining problem in v2: you do not know of one.

incident.rootCause: Since v2.31 (FLAG-298, Nov 12) the control plane API sends flag versions as strings. applyUpdate compares them with `msg.version > cur.version`, which for two strings is a lexicographic comparison, so "10" > "9" is false and the update is ignored as stale. new-checkout went from version 9 to version 10 for the first time at 10:02, so the kill switch was dropped on every node running v2.31. The v2.31 deploy was paused after 3 of 8 nodes (w-6, w-7, w-8) because of an unrelated latency alert, so nodes w-1 to w-5 still run v2.30, which compares numbers, and applied it. With a round-robin load balancer about a third of checkouts (3/8) still see the new flow, and the same user flips between old and new. It predates today: promo-banner crossed 9 to 10 on Nov 14 and nobody noticed because the 12:00 full resync healed it. The next resync is at 12:00 today. The client SDK cache (5 minutes) and the CDN are red herrings: new tabs also get the new checkout, and the stuck nodes keep answering on=true an hour later.
keyPoints: Uses evidence from the logs (sync.ignored with msg_version "10" against cached_version "9" on w-6, w-7 and w-8; eval.stats on>0 only on those nodes; the two versions v2.30 and v2.31; promo-banner on Nov 14 healed by the resync).
Pushes back on blaming the SDK or CDN and on the 'propagating' status message, with evidence (50 minutes is ten times the TTL, fresh tabs are affected).

Proposes a fast mitigation separately from the code fix: POST /admin/resync or flagshipctl resync --all on the stuck nodes (or a rolling restart), and does not resume the paused v2.31 deploy before the fix ships.

Fixes the compare: parse versions to numbers (and reject bad ones), only a strictly newer version replaces the cache, so late old messages are still ignored; a snapshot that fails to parse leaves the cache alone.
Writes a regression test for 9 to 10 and 99 to 100 that fails on the old code, plus out-of-order delivery.

Rulesets published to a CDN are public: allow lists (user ids, maybe staff emails), targeting rules, and unreleased feature names leak to anyone. Per-user and sensitive targeting must stay server side, or the ruleset must be reduced.
Bucketing must match byte for byte across JavaScript, Swift and Kotlin (hash, string encoding, integer overflow); a mismatch flips users between variants. Needs shared test vectors.
Old mobile apps never update, so the eval nodes cannot be shut down; two systems to run for a long time.
Version/ordering problems move to the client (stale rulesets, partial downloads, downgrades); keep monotonic versions and a way to force a refresh.
